title: We know the exact year Vikings were in North America: 1021
body: Wooden objects at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland were cut with metal tools, which local peoples did not have. A solar storm in the year 993 left a marker in tree rings worldwide. Counting rings outward from it showed the trees were felled in 1021.
takeaway: That is 471 years before Columbus crossed the Atlantic.
visual: a Viking longship beached on a rocky northern shore beside turf-roofed huts, a man splitting timber with an iron axe

title: An Indian king sent a fleet across the Bay of Bengal in 1025
body: Rajendra Chola I, ruling from what is now Tamil Nadu, launched a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire, more than 2,000 km away. His forces raided ports in Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula that controlled the sea trade between India and China.
takeaway: Tamil merchant guilds were active across Southeast Asia, and their inscriptions are still found there.
source: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri, The Colas (1955)
visual: a fleet of medieval South Indian sailing ships with tall prows crossing a stormy sea toward a jungle-fringed coast

title: A 2,000-year-old Greek device modelled the heavens with gears
body: Divers found the Antikythera mechanism in a shipwreck in 1901. Built around the second century BCE, it used at least 30 bronze gears to show the positions of the Sun and Moon, the phases of the Moon and the dates of eclipses.
takeaway: Nothing as mechanically complex is known again for more than a thousand years. Knowledge can be lost.
visual: a corroded bronze device of interlocking gears resting on the seabed among amphorae, shafts of light from above

title: The Mongols ran a relay post across Asia
body: The Mongol Empire, the largest connected land empire in history, set up stations called yam about a day's ride apart. Each kept fresh horses, food and lodging. Riders with urgent messages changed horses at each one and could cover around 200 km in a day.
takeaway: The same network sheltered merchants and envoys, which is how Marco Polo was able to cross Asia.
source: Thomas Allsen, Culture and Conquest in Mongol Eurasia (2001)
visual: a rider galloping across open steppe toward a small station of felt tents where fresh horses wait

title: One stone unlocked 3,000 years of Egyptian writing
body: The Rosetta Stone, found by French soldiers in 1799, carries the same decree of 196 BCE in three scripts: hieroglyphs, everyday Egyptian script and ancient Greek. Scholars could read the Greek. Jean-François Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
takeaway: Before 1822 nobody alive could read what the Egyptians had written about themselves.
visual: a dark slab of stone densely carved in three bands of different ancient script, lit by a scholar's candle

title: China sent giant fleets to Africa before Columbus was born
body: Between 1405 and 1433 the admiral Zheng He led seven voyages for the Ming emperor, with hundreds of ships and about 27,000 men. They reached India, Arabia and the coast of East Africa. Then the court ended the voyages and let the fleet decay.
takeaway: A state can abandon a lead it holds. Why China turned inward is still debated by historians.
source: Edward Dreyer, Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty (2007)
visual: an enormous many-masted Chinese treasure ship with red sails towering over smaller vessels on a calm tropical sea

title: After the Black Death, workers' wages rose
body: The plague of 1347 to 1351 killed an estimated third to half of Europe's people. With so few labourers left, survivors could demand more. In England real wages roughly doubled over the following century, despite laws that tried to hold pay down.
takeaway: Scarcity shifts bargaining power. Some historians link the labour shortage to the decline of serfdom in western Europe.
visual: a few medieval farm workers harvesting a wide golden field with many abandoned cottages in the background

title: Gandhi walked about 390 km to pick up a handful of salt
body: In March 1930 Mohandas Gandhi and 78 followers set out from Sabarmati Ashram. After 24 days they reached the sea at Dandi, where he gathered salt in defiance of a British law that taxed it and banned Indians from making their own. Over 60,000 people were jailed in the protests that followed.
takeaway: Salt was chosen because everyone, rich or poor, needed it. A simple, universal symbol made the cause easy to join.
visual: a long line of marchers in white homespun walking a dusty coastal road toward the sea at dawn, seen from behind

title: Railways are the reason clocks agree
body: Until the 1800s every town set its clocks by the local Sun, so noon in Bristol came about ten minutes after noon in London. Train timetables made that unworkable. Britain's railways adopted London time in 1847, and an 1884 conference made Greenwich the world's reference for time.
takeaway: India adopted a single standard time, five and a half hours ahead of Greenwich, in 1906.
visual: a Victorian railway station with a steam train at the platform beneath a large clock, a stationmaster checking a pocket watch

title: A king had 282 laws carved in stone 3,700 years ago
body: Hammurabi of Babylon ruled around 1750 BCE. His laws, cut into a black stone pillar more than two metres tall, cover theft, wages, divorce, building standards and doctors' fees. Many take the form: if someone does this, then that follows.
takeaway: Laws on public display could be checked against a written text. The pillar is now in the Louvre.
visual: a tall polished black stone pillar covered in fine wedge-shaped carving, a king and a seated god carved at its top
